content: Chronic hypertension refers to persistently elevated blood pressure levels, which can lead to significant health complications if left untreated. Blood pressure (BP) is the force exerted by circulating blood on the walls of arteries and is determined by two primary factors: cardiac output (CO) and systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Maintaining normal blood pressure is essential for ensuring adequate blood flow throughout the cardiovascular system. Clinically, blood pressure is one of the most critical vital signs to monitor. Hypertension (HTN) is typically defined as a systolic blood pressure (SBP) of 140 mmHg or higher and/or a diastolic blood pressure (DBP) of 90 mmHg or higher, measured on at least two separate occasions. However, lower target BP thresholds are recommended for certain populations, such as individuals with diabetes, significant proteinuria, or other renal diseases. Classification In 2004, the Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee (JNC 7) classified blood pressure into four categories: normal, prehypertension, stage I hypertension, and stage II hypertension. In contrast, the 2007 European Society of Hypertension (ESH) and European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines introduced a classification system with seven categories, which remained unchanged in their 2013 update. Unlike JNC 7, the ESH/ESC classification excludes the prehypertension category and instead includes three grades of hypertension. Pathophysiology The pathophysiology of secondary hypertension is well-documented, but the exact mechanisms underlying primary (essential) hypertension remain a topic of debate. It is now widely accepted that primary hypertension results from a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors, with varying contributions in different individuals. Causes Primary hypertension is far more prevalent than secondary hypertension, accounting for 90–95% of cases. When no specific cause can be identified after a thorough evaluation, the condition is classified as primary or essential hypertension. This is considered a chronic disease requiring lifelong management. Secondary hypertension, on the other hand, arises from identifiable underlying conditions such as obstructive sleep apnea, hyperaldosteronism, kidney diseases, excessive catecholamine production, coarctation of the aorta, or Cushing syndrome. Differentiating Hypertension from Other Conditions Before diagnosing primary hypertension, secondary causes must be excluded. Additionally, other conditions that can elevate blood pressure, such as white coat hypertension, masked hypertension, and pseudohypertension, should be considered. Epidemiology and Demographics Hypertension is a global epidemic and remains one of the most common chronic diseases. Surveys estimate its prevalence to be approximately 44% in Europe. The condition becomes more common with advancing age and is particularly prevalent among non-Hispanic Black individuals. Its prevalence is similar in men and women. Risk Factors Established risk factors for essential hypertension include advanced age, male sex, African American ethnicity, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, smoking, high dietary salt intake, obesity, and a sedentary lifestyle. Emerging risk factors are also being studied for their potential role in the development of hypertension. Screening The recommended age to begin screening for hypertension varies between 13 and 20 years, depending on the guidelines. Hypertension is generally defined as an SBP >140 mmHg and/or a DBP >90 mmHg. However, in certain populations, treatment may be initiated at lower BP thresholds. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis Hypertension is a well-established risk factor for serious diseases, including cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and renal conditions. Chronic uncontrolled hypertension can lead to target organ damage, most commonly affecting the heart, brain, kidneys, and retina. Even moderate elevations in blood pressure can reduce life expectancy. The risk of cardiovascular complications increases significantly with incremental rises in blood pressure. Blood pressure should be viewed as a continuum of risk rather than distinct stages, and its management should be integrated with other cardiovascular risk factors to determine the optimal treatment approach. Diagnosis History A detailed medical history is essential for diagnosing and assessing hypertension. This includes identifying symptoms of high blood pressure, evaluating risk factors, and assessing for target organ damage. In some cases, history-taking alone may reveal secondary causes, such as drug-induced hypertension, guiding individualized diagnostic and management strategies. Physical Examination In patients with isolated hypertension and no evidence of target organ damage, physical examination findings are often unremarkable except for elevated blood pressure. However, clinicians should carefully evaluate for signs of target organ damage and associated clinical conditions. Blood Pressure Measurement The most accurate method for diagnosing hypertension involves using a sphygmomanometer in a clinical setting. Proper technique, including appropriate device and cuff selection and patient positioning, is critical. Potential sources of error, such as those related to the device, patient, or technique, must be minimized. Ambulatory and self-measured blood pressure monitoring can also be valuable, particularly for follow-up. Laboratory Findings Laboratory tests are often performed to identify secondary causes of hypertension and assess for end-organ damage, such as to the heart, retina, or kidneys. Additional tests for diabetes and elevated cholesterol levels are conducted, as these are independent risk factors for cardiovascular disease and require management. Electrocardiography An electrocardiogram (ECG) is used to detect left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) or silent myocardial infarction, which may be associated with hypertension. Echocardiography Two-dimensional echocardiography can reveal signs of LVH and heart failure in hypertensive patients. Chest X-Ray A chest X-ray may show evidence of congestive heart failure, such as cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, or Kerley B lines. Treatment Lifestyle Modification Lifestyle changes are the cornerstone of initial hypertension management and are also critical for disease prevention. Recommended modifications include reducing dietary salt intake, achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, increasing consumption of fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy products, limiting alcohol intake, and engaging in regular aerobic exercise. While lifestyle changes can effectively control blood pressure in many patients, most will require two or more antihypertensive medications. Medical Therapy Pharmacologic therapy is the most effective way to lower both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in hypertensive patients. Guidelines from JNC 7 (2004) and ESH/ESC (2013) provide recommendations for medical therapy. Recent data have shifted away from the traditional use of thiazide diuretics as first-line therapy for isolated essential hypertension. Current guidelines support the use of any antihypertensive agent, with specific classes recommended for certain conditions or patient populations based on compelling indications.
